scope: United States nonprofit exhibition galleries and artist-run/cooperative spaces; non-NYC/Los Angeles geographic breadth prioritized.

methodology.tools: Context web-search, web-scrape, and submit-batch official-site Markdown scraping; batch results retained and reviewed in full, including complete artifact-backed payloads.
methodology.inclusion: Current/recent or forthcoming official exhibition evidence, or maintained operating gallery program. Museums, framing-only shops, grant-only programs, inactive/compromised sites and unverified candidates excluded. Temporary exhibition-installation closures do not imply permanent closure.
methodology.tiers: Qualitative operating-position estimates, not measured financial size. Nationally/regionally prominent nonprofit exhibition organizations are Medium / Mid-Tier; community/cooperative/independent spaces are Small / Boutique. No Large / Blue-Chip tier used.
methodology.organizations: One row per organization. Tiger Strikes Asteroid’s five U.S. cities combined. Artspace in Richmond and Artspace in Raleigh are distinct organizations and must not be merged solely by name.
methodology.activity_basis: official_dated_exhibition = explicit 2026/2027 exhibition dates; official_current_program = named current program or current exhibition with contextual date evidence; official_ongoing_gallery_program = operating gallery program verified but dated exhibition title not exposed. Each row documents the exact limitation.

limitations: Not a census and not exhaustive by state; the search prioritizes credible official evidence rather than filling a fixed quota.

Some maintained official pages expose no individual dated exhibition. These are explicitly tagged official_ongoing_gallery_program and should not be described as having a particular exhibition open on the check date.
Recent or forthcoming exhibitions establish organizational activity, not necessarily an exhibition open on November 15. Temporary installation closures are documented.
Legal nonprofit/tax status was not independently audited for every row; artist-run and artist-owned cooperatives are included under the assignment even when not themselves 501(c)(3) organizations.
Some pages returned navigation-only, failed, expired, or compromised content; exclusions are research limitations, not assertions that every such organization is permanently closed.

November 14, 2026
As we ease into the season of giving, we're reflecting on the ways the arts enrich our everyday lives. Some are easy to identify, like a beautifully curated gallery wall or a piece of pottery fresh out of the kiln. Others are less tangible, like the friendships formed in a classroom, the confidence gained from trying something new, or the chance to rediscover your inner child while playing in the studio. Here are five reasons we're especially thankful for the arts this season. 1. The spaces that bring people together Galleries, studios, classrooms, and community art centers offer places to gather, meet people, exchange ideas, and find a sense of belonging. At AVA, we're grateful to provide a space where people of all ages and backgrounds can come together, express themselves, and connect through creativity. 2. The artists who share their creativity with the world From established artists to someone picking up a paintbrush for the first time, we're grateful for the people who bring beauty, curiosity, and fresh perspectives into the world. Art takes countless forms, and we're thankful for those who make room in their lives to create, experiment, and share a little piece of themselves with others. 3. The opportunity to keep learning One of the wonderful things about art is that there's no finish line. No matter your age or experience, there's always a new material to explore, a technique to try, or something unexpected to discover. Art reminds us that we can be beginners at any stage of life, and that learning doesn't always have to be about getting something right. Sometimes, the best part is simply seeing where your curiosity takes you. 4. The way art helps us see things differently Art can challenge our assumptions, spark conversations, preserve stories, and introduce us to experiences outside our own. Sometimes, it gives us a moment to stop and appreciate something we might otherwise overlook. We're grateful for the ways art encourages us to stay curious, consider different perspectives, and see the world through someone else's eyes. 5. ## Quiet Migrations
Quiet Migrations follows the journey of searching for truth, not unlike the allegory of Plato’s Cave. Migrations also refers to movement in the natural world, where humans and animals move unbound by the illusions of borders. The work reflects on identity, in the perception of self and how our surroundings experience us. 
By layering old maps and migratory diagrams, Escobar’s work connects the seasonal routes of species like monarch butterflies with the quiet, often overlooked journeys of human migration.

Monica uses drawing, assemblage and music to create a deeply personal installation that illuminates a reality she did not fully see until her recent ADHD diagnosis and treatments.

**_Spinoffs_** is an exhibition of art influenced by textiles. From French tapestries to Japanese Ikat, Blackwork embroidery to Italian damask, Chinese grass-cloth to Ukrainian folk fabric, fiber from around the world serves as muse, sometimes with a shout and sometimes with a whisper. Paintings, digital art, and pyrography reference our collective consciousness of textile history in visual form. An appreciation of fiber and its offshoots unite the works in this eclectic showcase of styles.
##### Jennifer Pettu_s     S{t}imulation_
The work in **_S{t}imulation_** continues my exploration of labor, function, and materiality in an increasingly disconnected and overwhelming world. The rapid proliferation of AI shortcuts, where there is no manual skill required, is disheartening – and means putting hands to material is even more vital to my process. Whether it is a pen, a paintbrush, or a needle and thread, I am marking my journey, with all its human imperfections. I embellish non-traditional materials with riotous texture and color to challenge institutionalized art practices, but also to invite reflection on the ways we are literally losing touch with our environments.

I am a South African multi-disciplinary artist working across ceramics, embroidery, beadwork, collage and photography. Deeply tied to cultural heritage and storytelling I use traditional woman’s handcrafts in much of my practice. My work is informed by women’s knowledge – past and present. I play with contemporary dialogues of societies notions of self-identity and beauty moulded through mass media, and at the same, time try to make sense of ancient lost wisdoms.
I explore re-matriation and systemic violence and I try to envisage new relationships with the feminine and earth through ancestral knowledge and mythology which could have the potential for healing.

Undivine Time by Tia-Simone Gardner revisits 2026, compressing 365 days of lived experience, memory, and reflection into a single timeline: the exhibition's run. The project invites us to examine what has been forgotten, what was actively or necessarily forgotten, and what we are bound to remember. Central to this exploration is Undivine Time, a conceptual title directly inspired by Junauda Petrus's evocative writing.

## Christine Crook & Pete Fields
So here we are again. This is a house, and these are its clothes. If you are reading this, maybe you‘re paying attention and you’ve noticed the second installment of our adornment to this building we call The Front, an art gallery, an artist collective, a home. This time around, we got louder, more riotous, and decided to offer a full-throttle celebration of this special house, a house that welcomes everyone and offers a place to show and see the art we create in New Orleans.
Or maybe you didn’t notice this building enough before. Maybe the paint color isn’t bright enough, or maybe you just didn’t see a sign letting you know that this is The Front. The old sign had faded and peeled, and the new sign got painted over, and we wanted to make sure you saw this building again. So we dressed it up. And when I say dressed, I mean Fully Dressed, like a New Orleans po-boy, with everything on it, slathered in Duke’s, piled high with lettuce, pickles, and tomatoes. Because the secret ingredient is always more.
This work celebrates The Front, celebrates local art, and celebrates community. It was created by me, Christine Crook, and my husband, Pete Fields. This house has nurtured our creativity and our friendships. It has been a place where we have made things, seen things, met people, laughed, gathered, and become part of something bigger.
